newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Denktash sees progress in Cyprus talks.
newsitem.headline: Denktash sees progress in Cyprus talks.

text.p: Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash reported limited progress on Tuesday in talks in Switzerland aimed at ending the island`s 23-year partition.
Denktash spoke positively of his meetings with Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides since Monday at a hotel near the resort of Montreux and vowed to continue the five-day talks.
But he ruled out signing a joint declaration at the end of the U.N.-brokered talks and diplomats said there was no sign of breakthrough on the key issues such as territory and refugees.

"The talks were very useful and helped us to understand each other`s positions," Denktash told reporters when asked about progress in the negotiations chaired by U.N. special Cyprus envoy Diego Cordovez under a media blackout.
"Now, everything is being put on the table. A study which takes into account the views of both sides can be realised."
But he added: "We have told Cordovez that we will not sign a joint declaration."
The talks are the second round following last month`s meeting in Troutbeck, New York, aimed at reuniting the island under a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.
Cyprus has been divided since Turkey invaded its northern third in response to a coup in the capital Nicosia, engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.
There is deep-rooted antagonism between the two communities, estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government representing both sides split apart amid violence.
Denktash said he met Clerides for about an hour for formal discussions on Tuesday after a similar meeting on Monday. The two leaders had agreed to meet again on Wednesday.

Diplomatic sources close to the talks said Cordovez put a proposal to Denktash on Tuesday aimed at allaying Turkish Cypriot fears about European Union plans to start entry talks for Cyprus early next year.
Denktash on Sunday threatened to pull out of the talks over the EU move, which U.N. officials had hoped would produce extra pressure for a settlement.
On the table in Glion is a U.N.-drafted paper urging commitment to a sustained, open-ended negotiating process.
It proposes a new constitution and legal instruments on the key issues of territory, security, refugees and guarantees.

Denktash sees bi-zonality as a loose federation of two strong, federated states, each dominated by one community, while Clerides interprets it as two zones with no borders, one run by the Greek and the other by Turkish Cypriots, diplomats said.
Greek Cypriots want refugees displaced by the violence to be able to claim their houses in the north and to be free to settle anywhere on the island -- anathema to Turkish Cypriots.
Turkish Cypriots, who make up 18 percent of the population but control 37 percent of land, want political sovereignty and real power-sharing, which the Greek Cypriots oppose.
"It is a dialogue of the deaf," said one diplomat close to the talks.
If the talks fail, diplomats fear Cyprus will end up more divided than ever and threaten to become a flashpoint in the eastern Mediterranean amid a build-up of arms on both sides.
